Nuclear power leads India's deployment need, and its fleet grew from
; reactor control and safety instrumentation is a command path into it.
Control-system risk on a fleet that has to grow. The trade data mix reactors with generic boilers, so they say little about who supplies the control systems.
Trusted-source and certification rules for control and safety instrumentation, restrictions on remote access by untrusted vendors, and detection, patching and incident-response capacity.
Remote access to wind turbines and vehicles

Turbine controllers, park control and connected-vehicle software reach large energy assets and fleets from outside the country. India imports little of this hardware relative to the size of its economy.

Restrictions on remote access and over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors; trusted-source rules for the control layer and the hardware built around it; support for redesigns that separate the control layer, so the fence can shrink.

blocks.title: What India needs to deploy faster
blocks.alt: Bar chart of India's deployment need by technology, marking Accelerate and Watch and the main driver of each.

inlines.v: Deployment need by technology, with the largest of its measures: demand adequacy, the gap to national targets, or system need. Review cases, which rest on a single indicator of low confidence, are shown apart in grey and are not deployment priorities.

Coal power and gas networks also clear the bar, coal mainly on demand adequacy and gas on system need. Accelerate says the system needs more of what they provide; this analysis does not weigh them against clean sources. Recorded policy already ranks coal power among India's top deployment priorities. Geothermal power and heat reads Accelerate on fewer measures, with no geothermal supply step assessed, so it is a case to examine, not a priority.

High deployment priority does not imply high manufacturing priority: the configured build is infrastructure, permitting and procurement. Oil use also reads Accelerate, but on a single indicator of low confidence, use rising from
; it is a review case, shown apart. As a supply-side question only: India's supply-chain need in crude oil is
out of a hundred, and the configured answer for that Watch step is supply diversified toward trusted producers. EV adoption and clean hydrogen sit below the bar: worth watching, not forcing.

The largest gap is rare-earth refining: it is India's only Secure step, yet recorded measures barely reach it or the separation step beside it. Battery components rank well below cells in India's recorded support, though both are Catch Up cases on the same anchor. Coal, copper and bauxite mining rank among India's most protected steps, where the configured answer is diversified supply from trusted producers for coal and at most a specified capability floor for copper and bauxite. Deployment policy lags for gas networks. The nuclear gaps in the table rest on trade baskets that cannot tell reactor and fuel parts from boilers, so this brief does not treat them as priorities. Recorded measures also localize wafers and PV cells, which read Partner, but that call is a review case and is not settled here.

sections.title: Strategic agenda — what should India do next?

blocks.text: 1. Secure the rare-earth chain through a mixed domestic and allied build-out

inlines.v: Build separation and metal-making at home, starting from a small export foothold (about
of world exports, with no measurable share of world supply) and testing it with feasibility work before committing capacity. Build the step to magnets with allied makers such as
Germany, the United States, Japan and Mexico

through co-investment and offtake. Hold stocks sized to the time it takes to restore supply until trusted supply qualifies. Recorded policy barely reaches this step today, so it is the first gap to close.

blocks.text: 2. Catch up in battery cells and components with time-limited support tied to benchmarks

inlines.v: Tie production incentives, first-of-a-kind finance, workforce and supplier development and demand creation to benchmarks, and let support sunset if the gap does not narrow. Keep the gate open to joint ventures on terms that transfer capability. Bring support for components up to the level of cells.

blocks.text: 3. Keep the wind, solar and EV equipment base competitive as India's allied contribution

inlines.v: Wind turbines, blades, PV modules and EV drivetrains are positions to hold, not to rebuild. Back them with R&D, workforce and supplier development and finance for expansion tied to benchmarks, and welcome allied investment in new blade capacity (in the AIB,

blocks.text: 4. Put a high, narrow fence around control software

inlines.v: Set trusted-source and certification rules for battery management, inverter firmware, smart meters, grid control, turbine controllers, connected vehicles and reactor control. Restrict remote access and over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors, and replace untrusted control software in the installed base. Whether India's own equipment makers can supply the certified alternative is not measured here and should be tested first.

blocks.text: 5. Use development partnerships to bring battery cells and components to scale

inlines.v: Start with partners that share the need, such as
Spain, the United Kingdom, Australia and Chile

. Use project preparation, supplier development, skills and certification first, then development finance, guarantees, offtake and joint ventures as plants come on line. The objective is a trusted second source for partners and a durable industry at home.

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate storage, solar, wind, grid and nuclear power while keeping sourcing open

inlines.v: Deploy faster through infrastructure, permitting, interoperability and procurement; buy commodity hardware competitively from trusted suppliers, with trusted-supplier and security conditions on public deployment support and connected equipment. Gas turbines, conversion and enrichment, and coal and copper mining are not localization priorities: affordable, diversified access is.

Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;

Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed. A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar. Observed policy never decides a choice. The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.

Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence. They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.

India is a coalition partner, not a core member; the brief applies the same method as for core members. Both nuclear manufacturing steps rest on trade baskets that mix reactor and fuel lines with generic boiler and steam-turbine parts, which the shares cannot tell apart. Reactors and nuclear fuel parts are therefore not treated as established or emerging industries. The AIB nuclear seat rests on a trade line in nuclear special materials with no physical data. The AIB flags its wind-blade line as usable with caution: its trade headings are broad, and production is more concentrated than trade. India's rare-earth position rests on its exports of rare-earth compounds, about
of world exports, with no measurable share of world supply. Allied supply covers India's rare-earth need although trusted suppliers hold only
of world supply, and India's imports are modest, though the data do not show that as the reason.

steps lack the data for a call, including every geothermal supply step and green hydrogen manufacturing and most recycling. Recorded policy ranks clean hydrogen among India's priorities, but its deployment need reads low on a single indicator, so this brief does not settle that disagreement. Competitive Position ranks India among economies that already supply a step, so a zero means no measurable position. Policy alignment and protection are ranks within India, not levels. Partner lists name where allied capacity sits, which can include trading hubs, not who owns it.

India is a development recipient in this analysis (not high income). A Catch Up step qualifies when its capability anchor is corroborated beyond context signals, its evidence and confidence are sufficient, and the economy sits inside the AIB trust screen. On a step whose data describe different products, the anchor must also measure the product the need is about. The developed partners named are high-income economies whose own same step has a strategic reason for more trusted capacity: Partner, Secure with allied delivery, high need, allied supply short, or new allied capacity needed. A constraint is named only where the data observe its input; otherwise the table says the data do not cover it. India's Preserve steps are a commercial route (trade, offtake and investment), and steps whose position cannot be verified are review cases. This brief does not compare current aid to India with these steps.
